The one genuinely unsaid line, which destination a ward prescription takes when both a `dispense` and a `Medication administration` service exist (spec 04 vs 01 appendix "a second destination is a second `request` entry"), belongs in the Pharmacy or Admissions pack spec, not core.

settings-sweep: A medication cannot be held and resumed — Spec 04 built-later names it: "`hold`/`resume` on a medication (inpatient)". The specialist's fix is the spec's own plan (two `action` values, `status` gains `held`, a `schema_version` bump, the row keeps its id) and is additive. Meanwhile the IM clinic can express "hold metformin 48 h around contrast" as a `change` with `instructions_text` (the row stays, `started_on` survives, the medication list shows the instruction) or stop-then-start; both are awkward, neither breaks a rule. The only correction to the spec is the parenthesis: it is an outpatient need too (contrast, colonoscopy, AKI), so schedule it with the Internal medicine pack rather than with admissions. Not before Phase 0: `patient_medications.status` is text and `action` is a JSON-schema enum, both widen as supersets.

settings-sweep: Emergency: five-level acuity, unknown patients and merge — The specialist already concedes acuity (03 appendix Y6: "a `triage` entry in the record; `priority` is its three-level shadow set by routing; a five-level order is the emergency pack's screen"). Unknown patients need no schema change: `register_patient` takes `given_name = 'Unknown'`, `sex = other`, and an estimated year — 03 appendix: "An age typed at the desk is stored as the year", "a year-only date is right to within six months" — which is exactly what every ED does and what `age_on` was designed for; the real date arrives later as a `patient_changes` row. `born_on NULL` would weaken a CHECK and `age_on` for no gain. `merge_patients` and `unmerge_patient` are spec 03 built-later with their refusal (`visit_open`) and read rule (`patient_id = ANY(ids)`) already written; "ship before any ED goes live" is scheduling, not a gap, and an ED is not among the owner's named packs.

settings-sweep: Mother-baby, twins and guardians: cross-patient links live in packs, and erase does not tell them — The specialist's own fix is "None to the record". Spec 01 rule 2 "No pointer in a record table crosses patients" is what sends `obstetrics.births (mother_patient_id, baby_patient_id)` to the pack schema, which spec 06 rule 5 allows ("holding core ids with no foreign key"). Each side's entry copies the other's record number into its own `data` (self-contained rule), and two `write_set`s for a delivery is by design — "`write_set(items)` writes one patient's signed set" — with the outbox replaying both. `erase_patient` telling packs is spec 02 built-later, to land with the first pack that stores another patient's id; a dangling id in a pack table after erase is harmless by construction (no key, no join from core). Guardian consent is `contact_text` until `patient_access`. Nothing here is a core gap.

settings-sweep: Sessions every other day and the fourteen-day join — Agreed with the specialist: a visit is whereabouts, a session is a clinical fact. Spec 03 rule 1 "A return joins the open visit" applies only while the visit is open; a dialysis or physiotherapy pack writes each session as an entry (`dialysis_session` with `values[]`) and ends the visit with `mark_visit(done)` — allowed from `pending` too ("closes it whatever is out; results still reach to-review") — so Wednesday's Here inserts a new row and the session count from entries is right. The printed `arrived_at` is a known limit the pack's screen replaces with `present_at`. No core change now or later.

settings-sweep: A pack cannot annotate a core entry — Expressible today two ways. A companion entry of the pack's own type in the same `write_set`, linked by `written_with_id` ("every member carries it"), with the pack's renderer drawing it under the prescription card — this keeps core JSON schemas closed, which is the point of spec 04 rule 1. Or plain text where text is right: `instructions_text` "15 mg/kg at 12.4 kg" on the prescription, and laterality in the request's question once the non-consult refusal (gap 2) is struck. Spec 01 rule 1 "A new fact is a key in `data`" was always a statement about core's own schemas; a pack extending a core type's schema would be exactly the cross-pack coupling spec 06 forbids. Revisit only if three packs ship the same companion.

settings-sweep: Outreach, home visits and telehealth: address, phone screen and the patient's own readings — All three parts are stated later rules or already permitted. Home visits are in scope by definition (spec 03: present is "at the door of a home visit"); the nurse marks Here and writes vitals from a phone (spec 05: "Reception, Here, vitals and the queue work on a phone"), and the address lives in `contact_text` today. `address_text` is listed in spec 03 built-later as an "additive nullable column with no rule on them" and lands with the first outreach department; returning it on `read_visit_queue` rows is a read change. A read-only RECORD region on a phone is a screen concern inside spec 05's own known limit ("The visit screen needs a tablet or larger"), not a data gap. Patient-sent readings are spec 01 rule 6 ("home readings" as non-final replies) gated by `patient_access` (spec 02 built-later); until then staff transcribe, which is an honest v1 the specialist accepts. Nothing here touches Phase 0.

workflow-sweep: Conditional and protocol orders ('if K < 3.0 give KCl 20 mmol') — Agree with the specialist. 01 naming: 'Not used in the schema: … order'; the record stores acts, not rules. A protocol is a template ('A template expands to N write_request calls inside one write_set'), a standing order is the nurse writing the act with the doctor's responsible_id ('Supervised orders carry responsible_id'; 'A user may write type T with responsible_id = X only if X may write T'), a recurrence is 'HbA1c in three months … sits in the upcoming view' (01 appendix 'Future orders') re-issued on reply, and PRN/home monitoring is 'a standing request whose readings are non-final replies'. Storing executable conditions or schedules in requests is exactly the speculative structure the owner rejects and where incumbents' order logic rots. One caveat that belongs to gap 1, not here: the responsible_id this path relies on is missing from every spec 04 signature and must be exposed when the signatures are settled.

abstraction-stress: Packs have no time-driven reaction path — Already handled by stated rules. Spec 01 appendix line 196: 'Anything time-dependent, such as expired, is computed by the read function'; line 470: 'The age of review_needed_at gives escalation of unreviewed critical results, with no new schema'; read_queue(is_upcoming) shows what is due; the queue footer counts to-review 'in red when a critical is waiting' (spec 05). Overdue, expiring and due are all boards someone opens, which is how a 50-patient clinic and most wards run. What the specialist actually wants is push notification, which appears nowhere in 01–06 and is not required to run either target setting. When a notification pack exists, packs.is_called_hourly plus <pack>.every_hour(organization_id) under the existing runner is one boolean, one function and one line in B11's cron.job set — additive, and correctly left until a real pack asks.

abstraction-stress: Cohort and recall queries have no gate — Handled by a stated later rule three times over: spec 01 known limits 'in-record search only'; spec 01 'Written as rules now, built later … cross-patient search (a derived table)'; appendix line 624 'Cross-patient search and cohort queries are later derived tables'; and spec 02 built-later 'erase_patient telling packs', which is exactly the register-cleanup the specialist worries about. The specialist is right that a pack cannot do it alone (no SELECT on patient_problems or entry_values), so read_cohort with a new action read:cohort and one index is core work — but it is a new function, a new action row and an index, all additive, and it lands naturally with the Internal medicine pack that first needs a recall list. Nothing in Phase 0 changes to make room for it.

abstraction-stress: Transfer needs department_id on mark_visit_routing; wards cannot open — Every element the specialist lists is already a stated later rule in spec 03: 'admissions: admitted as one ADD VALUE, a transfer as a routing step {department_id} on the same visit, beds in the admissions table by visit_id'; open_visit's not_yet (ward) is the placeholder that path removes; the sweep already skips wards 'a WHERE that matches nothing today and cannot be forgotten when admissions ship' (appendix line 123); and 'Meanings that never change' explicitly permits additive columns. The public function shape is not blocked either: spec 06 test 10 says the golden file 'gains lines and never loses one', and a five-parameter overload of mark_visit_routing — or, better named, mark_visit_transfer(visit_id, department_id, reason), since a transfer is a distinct act with a reason — is a gained line, not a removed one. Adding department_id now would force deciding the visits_open collision rule, is_first recomputation and the ward open path today, which is the speculative structure the owner rejects. Decide it with the admissions pack.

abstraction-stress: Shared care across organizations — Agreed with the specialist, and it is not a gap by the stated criterion: spec 01 known limits says 'no cross-organization record', spec 01 appendix says the organization 'is the boundary of sharing' and spec 06 test 6 raises on every cross-organization id. This is the deliberate choice that makes the closed record (rule 2), the tenant matrix (B16) and database-per-organization scale-out possible. A network that wants one record is one organization with sites (spec 02 site_name and served_departments); everything else is export and import as source = outside with stated_author_name and stated_recorded_at, which the appendix already names ('FHIR export (stable ids)'). A future messaging pack is the right home and needs nothing from core now.

abstraction-stress: The machine-user rule excludes non-reply machine writes — Already handled by a stated rule the specialist missed: spec 02 appendix line 49 'write_entry refuses a machine entry that is not a reply to an open request whose to_department_id is that department, unless it is a draft'; line 179 'writes replies to open requests sent there, or drafts'; line 379 'A point-of-care device that files unsolicited results drafts them for a clinician to commit'; spec 01 appendix line 214 'Machine output meant for one clinician stays here until that clinician commits it'. So the BP kiosk and the AI scribe both draft (data.drafted_with) and a nurse or doctor commits, which is also the clinically right author. The one true omission is cosmetic and additive: spec 01's function list names no draft functions although drafts is a table and 'the app never touches tables', and spec 05 rule 3 autosaves drafts. The client needs save_draft / read_drafts / discard_draft when it is built, after Phase 0's migrations; naming them then adds functions and changes nothing.

abstraction-stress: Packs never see visits, so bed state is client-driven — Agreed with the specialist. Spec 03 boundary 4 is deliberate: 'Packs never see visits … no pack executes a visit function — the client calls open_visit as the desk user and hands the id to the pack', and it is what keeps visits clinically empty and a pack unable to block the desk. The two-call discharge is handled by spec 05's outbox ('writes go into an IndexedDB outbox with their client ids and replay in order on reconnect'), so a dropped connection replays admissions_release_bed after mark_visit(done); and the bed board's truth is read_visit_queue plus the admissions table by visit_id — a bed whose visit has ended is free by derivation, the same pattern as BACK. Nothing to add.

abstraction-stress: No language convention on an entry — Stated later rule in two places: spec 04 'display lines in English in v1 (a display_line is data; translation is a client concern later)' and spec 05 built-later 'translation of display lines'; spec 03 already reserves language_name as an additive nullable column on patients. Typed text (text, *_text) is in whatever language the clinician types today, so a bilingual clinic runs. A language_code data key and a translation_of_id key are conventions in the data-key list, not structure, and can be added with the first translation feature; a translation of a discharge letter is meanwhile a note with files[] and text naming what it translates. The only thing worth noting for naming is that a language is a code, not a name, so when spec 03's reserved column is built it should be language_code, consistent with the specialist's proposal.

safety-regulatory: `born_on` carries no time of birth: neonatal ranges by hour of life cannot be expressed — Speculative for the first two years of an internal-medicine-first system, and nothing in Phase 0 forecloses it: `patients.born_at timestamptz` is a nullable additive column and a second `age_on` overload is additive. The unit of `service_field_ranges.age_low/age_high` is not a Phase 0 decision either: 02's decide-now places that table "with the Laboratory pack", so it is created later, where the unit (fractional days) is a fresh column, not a change. An hour-of-life bilirubin nomogram is a chart a neonatal pack computes, not a reference range that core's once-computed `flag` should ever try to express.

safety-regulatory: Tamper evidence stops at the trigger; scanned documents carry no hash — The owner already decided this: 01 appendix T11 "sha256 is declined until someone needs it", with the insert-only bucket, the path rule and the off-site copy as the file evidence. The Phase 0 argument fails twice. First, `write_entry` cannot compute a digest: the bytes live in Storage and the database never reads them, so the hash would be client-supplied, and a client-supplied hash proves nothing about the bytes. Second, a hash stored in the same database gives no protection against the named threat (a `postgres` role rewriting rows); only the off-site copy does. If integrity checking is ever wanted it is a nullable `entry_files.sha256` filled by the upload path, additive, with old rows NULL, no rewrite. `pgaudit` and MFA on the dashboard are operations, not spec. "core-before-phase-0" is wrong.

scale-operations: Go-live renumbers every patient — This reopens a decision the spec took twice: 03 appendix invariant 11 '`record_number` is minted from `core.record_numbers` on insert only and has no parameter', and line 291's rejections list 'an importer-typed number' by name. The stated path is line 50: 'a legacy import restarts one organization's series with one UPDATE by migration. Old numbers land in `patient_identifiers` as `record_number:<old system>`', and `read_patients` tries identifier values first, so the desk and every crosswalk find people by the old number. A hospital that must keep its MRN as the card number gets that without a parameter: the import is a migration-level script (the appendix's own words), it positions `core.record_numbers.last_number` to `legacy - 1` before each insert in ascending legacy order, and `register_patient` mints the legacy number from the counter; gaps in the legacy series become gaps in the counter, and `UNIQUE (organization_id, record_number)` still holds. A 500k-patient hospital with 30 interfaced systems is speculative for the first two years; the clinic's paper cards get a new number on the next visit. If counter-positioning is judged too ugly when the day comes, a defaulted importer-only parameter is a signature that grows, but nothing about it is Phase 0. The specialist's fallback, one known-limits sentence in spec 03 ('an import renumbers; old numbers are identifiers'), is worth writing.

scale-operations: Reporting has no home — The specs state the mechanism and the timing: spec 01 rule 1 'a new question is a derived table', its built-later list 'cross-patient search (a derived table)', 01 appendix line 624 'Cross-patient search and cohort queries are later derived tables', and 03 appendix line 83 'Reports (door-to-doctor = `seen_at - arrived_at`, left-without-being-seen = `left`, lapse rate) come from `visits` and `visit_steps` alone'. The specialist is right that a pack can never build these (spec 06 rule 4 'no privilege on any core table (not even a row lock)'), so the home must be core's; the stated rule already puts derived tables in core, and a `reporting` schema, a `reporter` role with SELECT on it alone, and a `read:report` action are all additive whenever the first report is wanted. Severity is wrong: no hospital reports from a transactional clinical core; it reports from a replica or a warehouse, and the owner is a clinician-developer with SQL on a Supabase read replica for year one. Worth one sentence now in spec 06 known limits ('a pack has no reporting access to core data; reports are core's derived views') so a pack author never asks for SELECT. Nothing in Phase 0.

scale-operations: Sites as labels: a hospital's administration is rows per department — The spec already states the later rule and the reason for waiting: spec 02 built-later 'a `sites` table when a site needs an address', 02 appendix line 74 'A `sites` table is additive when a site needs its own address', O15 'a `sites` table later', and line 356 explicitly rejects 'A `sites` table now'. Three sites and forty departments is speculative for the first two years, and even then 'the admin's day' is thirteen `served_departments` rows per reception entered once through the `save_…` loop the client already runs for presets (spec 02 'the client loops `save_…` with minted ids'). A nullable `site_id` on `served_departments` and `user_roles` read beside NULL is the additive column the spec's own rule permits when the rows become a chore. Nothing touches Phase 0.

scale-operations: The reception at scale is N queue calls and 300 chart prefetches — 03 appendix line 115 chose the N-call form deliberately: 'there is no `department_id = NULL` form and no cross-department order to define'. Forty indexed queries over `visits_present (department_id)` per burst on ten desks is nothing to Postgres, and a ten-desk forty-department central desk is speculative for two years; a nullable `department_id` is additive the day it is wanted. The '300 chart prefetches' do not happen: `read_record` is gated by `read:record` (02 appendix line 51), no spec grants it to the receptionist, reception 'is clerical by the gate' (spec 03), and search 'is not a record read' (rule 6); spec 05's prefetch sentence is written for 'the 30 open charts of a clinic'. Scoping prefetch to screens that open charts is a client convention, the same one-sentence fix gap 1 already needs.

scale-operations: Bed state cannot follow the visit — The specialist's own placement is right ('Nothing in core') and spec 03 boundary 4 already states the pattern he wants documented: 'no pack executes a visit function — the client calls `open_visit` as the desk user and hands the id to the pack'. One correction to his fix: a pack's `after_write` cannot reconcile from `read_visit_queue(ward)`. The pack role may EXECUTE public `read_…` functions, but the gate inside runs as the `pack:<key>` user, whose role 'holds `mark:held` and the pack's own actions only' (02 appendix line 52, enforced by B16); `read:queue` is a core action it does not hold, so the call raises. Reconciliation belongs on the pack's ward screen, which the shell hands `{ department, queue, openVisit, openRequest }` (spec 06 client side) as the staff user: a bed whose visit is no longer present or open is freed through the pack's own `admissions_free_bed`, and the discharge `note`, an entry with its `visit_id` that `after_write` does see, frees it server-side; a death is a discharge note too. Write that as the worked example in spec 06 when the admissions pack is specced; no core rule moves.

developer-readiness: JSON schema location, validation engine and where `schema_version` lives are unspecified — The write functions already do the validation a schema engine would: every `write_<type>` takes typed parameters and 'only validates and shapes `data`' (01 appendix), so `data` never arrives from the client as a blob; `pg_jsonschema` and a `core.entry_type_schemas` table would validate what the function itself just built. The JSON schemas serve the client (TS types) and the golden fixtures (CI); two generators is normal (`supabase gen types` for signatures, schema-to-TS for `data`), which is what spec 05's 'generated from the database' and spec 04's 'from the same schemas' each describe. `schema_version` lives in `data` by the closed-columns rule plus 'the renderer reads both'; nowhere else is possible. Where the schema files sit is repo layout.

developer-readiness: Test harness tooling, golden-fixture format and a dev seed path are unnamed, and MFA blocks scripted seeding — Tooling and fixture formats are repo decisions, not spec content; nothing in 01–06 forbids pgTAP, vitest or any layout, and B14 already fixes the one path that matters (`supabase/tests/fixtures/`). The MFA objection dissolves on Supabase: `aal` is a JWT claim, and a seed sets `request.jwt.claims` the way every Supabase seed does, so the gate is exercised, which is the specialist's own conclusion. Write it in the README when the first test is written.

developer-readiness: Main specs and appendices disagree on columns; `erasures` is in no table list; `entry_types.pack` is `'core'` in one spec and NULL in another — The precedence is stated where the reader starts: the 01 appendix header ('Where the two differ, 01-record.md wins') and the README ('later specs build on it'). Applied: the main spec's one-line column lists are abbreviations, not conflicts, so `entry_values` carries `organization_id` and `source`; `codes` already has `organization_id null` in the appendix; `drafts` has the appendix's columns; `erasures (patient_id, reason, actor_id, erased_at)` is in the appendix's 'Outside the record' section and its table-kinds row; `write_entered_in_error(id, replaces_id, reason_text)` is spec 04's, later and suffix-correct. The one true conflict, `entry_types.pack = 'core'` (04) versus `coalesce(entry_types.pack, 'core')` (02), is forced by the `actions.pack null → packs.key` pattern: NULL, no `packs` row for core, a one-word fix in 04. `organization_id` on `erasures` is additive.

developer-readiness: Schema placement (`core` vs `public`) is defined only in an amendment file, and the gates' schema is unstated — It is defined, and normatively: 02-organization.spec01-changes.md item 16 is the amendment the 01 appendix header points to ('The exact list is in 02-organization.spec01-changes.md'), and spec 02's main text already shows the split ('for packs: `core.write_entry` · `core.change_request` · `core.record_settings_change` · public `read_…` · public `mark_…`'); `require_access` and `current_user_id` are private functions, so `core` by 'every table and private function lives in schema `core`'. Spec 06's bare `entry_types` sits in the same code block as `after_write(entry core.entries)`, so the missing `core.` prefix is a typo to fix in 06 when gap 2's template is corrected. PostgREST exposing exactly `public` is already B9 ('no core table is in a PostgREST-exposed schema').

developer-readiness: RLS backstop and Realtime topic naming are one sentence each; `security definer` bypasses RLS unless FORCE is chosen — The design forces the answers. FORCE is impossible: every access is a `security definer` function owned by the core owner, and FORCE would subject that owner to the policy and break every funnel; 'backstop' (01 invariant 14) can only mean ENABLE on every `core` table with one membership policy for `authenticated`, behind zero grants, and a developer who tried FORCE would learn it from the first fixture. The topic names `record:<patient>` and `queue:<department>` are locked in spec 01 and need no organization prefix: the `realtime.messages` policy joins `core.patients` or `core.departments` to the membership InitPlan, evaluated at channel join. Adding 'every core table has RLS enabled' to B9 is a test line, not a spec change.
